Hymenophore: In the form of ridges running deeply down the stem. They are dichotomously branched and joined by transverse anastomoses. They are yellow-orange, often with a pink tinge, and are wavy, so that they resemble wrinkles. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness up to 2.5 cm, firm, yellow. The shape is cylindrical, in the upper part it widens conically, passing smoothly into the cap. Flesh: Pale yellow, resilient and firm. Spore print: White or yellowish. Spores smooth, elliptical, measuring 4–6.5 × 7–11 μm. Similar species: It differs in the absence of a violet tomentum on the cap and has less wavy and less forked ridges.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland it is rare. It occurs mainly in beech forests and mountain spruce forests. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in forests, mainly in grass and on fallen leaves, especially of such species as birches, beeches, oaks, less often pines.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: The underground part of the thallus, the mycelium, is usually invisible, whereas the fruiting bodies with basidia producing spores grow above the layer of moss on the forest floor. Cap: Diameter 1–12 cm. In young fruiting bodies button-like, round in shape, later convex with an inrolled margin, and in older specimens expanded, funnel-shaped and irregular. The colour is light yellow to orange-yellow. The surface is smooth, matt. Hymenophore: In the form of irregularly and dichotomously branched, thick ridges running far down the stem. They are the same colour as the cap. They are often joined by anastomoses. Stem: Height 3–6 cm, diameter up to 2.5 cm. The colour of the cap, often a lighter shade. The base is narrowed, above it wider and gently passing into the cap. Solid, firm and often curved. Flesh: White or pale yellow, of compact consistency, brittle, fibrous in the stem. The smell is fruity, spicy, slightly peppery. The taste is mild, sour or slightly sharp. Spore print: Whitish, yellowish or light ochre-yellow. Spores measuring 7–11 × 4–6.5 µm, colourless, ellipsoid in shape, smooth. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species. Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is common and is among the most frequently occurring forest fungi. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in deciduous and coniferous forests, often on sandy, acidic soils. Often under spruces among moss. In some regions of Europe, however, it is disappearing. It is becoming increasingly rare, as a result of acid rain, e.g. in Germany. Long-term scientific studies carried out in the Netherlands have shown that its numbers are not affected by the collecting of its fruiting bodies by mushroom pickers.
Cantharellus pallens Pilát is a species of fungus in the family Hydnaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–8 cm. In young specimens arched, then flat, finally funnel-shaped, fleshy. The margin is lobed, wavy, blunt; the surface is coloured from white to yellowish, often whitish or yellowish variegated. Hymenophore: Ridged (phlebioid). The ridges are low and forked, running deeply down the stem and of the same colour. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness up to 3 cm, firm, widening upward and gradually passing into the cap. The surface is bare, smooth and of the same colour as the cap. Flesh: Fleshy, whitish, not changing colour when damaged, with a slight spicy smell and a delicately stinging taste. Spore print: Cream, cream-yellowish. Spores ellipsoid with a hilar appendage, smooth, hyaline, with granules and guttules, 8–9 × 4.5–5 µm. Similar species: It prefers more acidic soils and coexists with more tree species: beech, birch, oak, spruce and pine. Cantharellus amethysteus has various yellow colours with a violet to amethyst tinge. It also prefers acidic soils and occurs under deciduous trees, including oak, beech and birch, but sporadically also under coniferous trees.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Europe it is widely distributed. Its localities have also been reported in Russia, Japan and North America. In Poland one locality was reported up to 2003, further ones in later years. Current localities are also given by the online mushroom atlas. It is included there in the list of threatened species worthy of protection. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It occurs in deciduous forests, usually under beeches and lindens.
Cerioporus squamosus (Huds.) Quél. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 10–40 cm. Young ones almost flat with an inrolled margin, older ones slightly funnel-shaped; covered with dark brown scales on a whitish to light brown background (looking from the centre to the outside of the cap). Tubes: Irregular, angular, white/cream pores, the smaller the further from the stem, 1–2.5 mm in diameter, decurrent. Stem: Most often lateral, short and stocky, with the tubes passing smoothly from the cap onto the stem. At the top usually white or dirty flesh-coloured, at the bottom covered with a brown-black or black tomentum. Flesh: White, with a faint taste and a mealy-cucumber smell. It is juicy-fleshy, and after drying it becomes light, cork-like and brittle. Spore print: White. Spores oblong-elliptical, smooth, measuring 10–13 × 4–5 µm. Similar species: Polyporus tuberaster. The fruiting body is much smaller (up to 15 cm in diameter). The cap is funnel-shaped, the stem central.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs commonly throughout Poland (except the higher parts of the mountains). It occurs in forests, parks, gardens, in thickets and by roads. It grows on living and dying trunks of deciduous trees, rarely coniferous. It occurs on trees almost all year round; young fruiting bodies appear in March and develop until the first frosts, and overripe fruiting bodies persist on trunks sometimes even until February. It develops most often on beeches, maples and ash trees.
Cerioporus varius (Pers.) Zmitr. & Kovalenko is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–10 cm, round or kidney-shaped, convex in young specimens, flatly expanded in older ones. The surface is smooth and bare. The margin of the cap is sometimes wavy. The colour in young specimens is fawn-red or cinnamon, in older ones grey-yellow. Tubes: Small, 0.1–0.2 mm in diameter and 0.5–1.5 mm long, running down one side of the stem. They form only one layer. The pores are initially white, in older specimens brownish. Stem: Height 0.5–2 cm, thickness 0.5–1.5 cm. It usually grows laterally. In the upper part it is the same colour as the cap, in the lower part, however, it is black. Flesh: White, with a faint smell and a somewhat bitter taste. Spore print: White. Spores cylindrical or sausage-shaped, smooth, measuring 10–7 × 2–3.5 μm. A species with fairly high morphological variability. Individual specimens differ quite significantly in colour and cap shape. In dry weather its development often stops and the pores take on a brown colour. Similar species: Picipes melanopus. It has a dark brown and suede-like cap; Picipes badius has an entirely black stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America and in Europe. In Poland it is common, especially in the mountains. The fruiting bodies appear from June to October on various species of deciduous trees. Its occurrence has been found on the following trees: Fagus, Acer negundo, Alnus, Betula pendula, Quercus robur, Quercus sp., Salix caprea, Ulmus minor. It is a saprotroph; by decomposing dead wood it causes white rot of wood.
Chalciporus piperatus (Bull.) Bataille is a species of fungus belonging to the family Boletaceae (Suillaceae).

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–5, exceptionally up to 7 cm. Cushion-shaped in young specimens, somewhat flattened in older ones. The skin is smooth, orange-brown in colour. In wet weather it is greasy. Tubes: Fairly short, adnate or slightly decurrent on the stem. They are rusty-brown in colour. The pores are darker, brick-brown in colour, with a coppery shade. They are large, angular and have uneven edges. Stem: Height 2–6 cm, diameter 0.4–1 cm. It has the same colour as the cap, only lighter (yellowish) in the lower part. It is cylindrical, equally thick along its whole length, or slightly narrowed at the bottom, solid, sometimes slightly curved. Flesh: Cream in the cap, yellow or lemon-yellow in the stem. It has a faint smell and a sharp, burning taste. Spore print: Brown. Spores smooth, spindle-shaped, measuring 3–4 × 8–12 μm. Similar species: Suillus variegatus is similar in appearance, but it is distinctly larger and does not have such a burning taste. The similar Boletinus cavipes is easy to distinguish by its hollow stem and disappearing ring. It has a somewhat bitter taste, but not as burning as Chalciporus piperatus.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents and on many islands. In Central Europe it is fairly common. A terrestrial parasitic fungus. It occurs mainly in coniferous and mixed forests, under common juniper, silver fir, silver birch, beech, Norway spruce and Scots pine, always in the company of Amanita species, among others Amanita muscaria and Amanita regalis, on whose mycelia it is parasitic. The fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn.
Chlorophyllum olivieri (Barla) Vellinga is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 46–130 mm, spherical in young fruiting bodies, umbrella-shaped and grey in older ones, covered with small scales of a colour similar to the skin of the cap. In the middle a large patch coloured from brown to red-brown. Gills: White, free, fairly crowded, 1–7 mm away from the stem. They turn red when damaged. With age they become beige. Stem: Height 80–190 mm, thickness 7–13 mm, smooth, whitish to light beige, ending in a bulb. The ring is movable, double. Flesh: Whitish, turning red-yellow or orange when damaged, red with age. The smell is earthy or mushroomy, the taste unpleasant. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, ellipsoid, measuring 8–11 × 5.5–7 μm. Similar species: Chlorophyllum rhacodes – occurs rather in parks, its cap is lighter and the scales on it are not so distinctly overlapping. The colour of its discolouration is more red-orange, whereas the discolouration of Ch. olivieri is more yellow-orange.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Widely distributed in Europe and fairly common. It also occurs in Poland. It is very often confused with Chlorophyllum rhacodes, which makes it hard to confirm localities. In the 2003 checklist of large-fruited basidiomycetes of Poland this species was not included. Probably at that time its representatives were commonly taken for Chlorophyllum rhacodes. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests.
Chlorophyllum rhacodes (Vittad.) Vellinga is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 8–15 cm, spherical in young fruiting bodies, umbrella-shaped in older ones. The skin is grey-brown or brown and is covered with fibrous, whorled, brownish, darker and distinctly spreading scales. Gills: White, sometimes with drops of liquid on them; after drying they change colour to olive-green. Under pressure they turn red. Stem: Height up to 15 cm, thickness 1–1.5 cm. At the base it widens into a bulb; almost smooth, initially white, with time becoming browner, without a trace of striations. Under the cap there is a white ring that can be moved along the stem. When damaged it turns reddish. Flesh: Whitish, turning orange-ochre when damaged. The taste is mild, without smell. Spore print: White. Spores smooth, ellipsoid, measuring 9–12 × 6–7 μm. Similar species: Leucoagaricus nympharum, with a more slender and delicate fruiting body covered with white scales. It also differs in its flesh, which is white and changes colour only slightly when damaged (reddens slightly).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and New Zealand. In Central Europe it is common, in Poland as well. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It grows at forest edges, in parks and in woodland clearings in deciduous and coniferous forests.
Chondrostereum purpureum (Pers.) Pouzar is a species of fungus belonging to the family Cyphellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Width 1–3 cm, spread out or spread out with reflexed margins. It attaches to the substrate by its side, and often part of the fruiting body stands away from the substrate. It often occurs in groups, and then the fruiting bodies overlap like roof tiles. The surface is felty, coloured from whitish to grey. The hymenophore is smooth, waxy, zoned, in various shades of violet, purple and brown. Flesh: Elastic, without smell. It is layered and darkest just under the upper surface, lightest in the middle. Spores: Colourless, almost cylindrical, sometimes slightly curved, measuring 5–8 × 2.5–3 (exceptionally up to 5) μm. Similar species: Auricularia mesenterica. It differs in the colour of the underside (it is dark brown), it is rubbery, elastic and always forms a cap. Veluticeps abietina also has a violet fruiting body, but it is firmer, darker, much rarer (it occurs here and there in the Carpathians, the Sudetes and the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed across the globe. In Poland it is very common. It occurs commonly in forests, parks, thickets, by roads, in gardens. The fruiting bodies grow on branches, trunks and stumps, on both dead and living wood, mainly of deciduous trees, rarely on coniferous trees. It grows mainly on damaged places. It can most often be met on the cut surface of trunks and stumps. The fruiting bodies grow throughout the year, but most often in autumn and during a mild winter.
Chroogomphus rutilus (Schaeff.) O.K. Mill. is a species of fungus in the family Gomphidiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–15 cm. Convex with an inrolled margin when young, coppery-brown, later somewhat faded; flattened when old; when wet – strongly slimy, when dry – smooth and shiny; very thick and fleshy. Young fruiting bodies are enclosed in a cobweb-like veil. Gills: First coppery-grey, dark purple-brown when ripe; very thick and sparse; often forked and running far down the stem. Stem: Long and slender, fleshy, coppery-orange to yellow-brownish, with a delicate zigzag pattern from the ochre veil, when dry sometimes with a thickened ring zone. Flesh: Orange-yellow, after pressing, after some time, stained carmine. At the base of the stem chrome yellow; without smell and with a mild taste. Spore print: Olive-black. Spores elongated, ellipsoid-spindle-shaped, smooth, brown-yellow, 17–23 × 5.5–7 µm. Similar species: Chroogomphus helveticus, which has a felty cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed in North America and Europe, and its localities have also been reported in Korea and Japan. In Poland it is common. It grows in coniferous and mixed forests, on the ground, under silver fir, Scots pine and dwarf mountain pine. The fruiting bodies appear from July to November.
Clathrus archeri (Berk.) Dring is a species of fungus in the family Phallaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Initially ovoid, conical or pear-shaped, enclosed in a covering. This is the so-called egg. It is 3.5–6 cm high, 2.5–5 cm in diameter, white-grey in colour and partly sunk into the substrate. During its development the covering in the upper part of the egg splits and a banana-shaped receptacle emerges. The receptacle reaches a height of 5–15 cm and on reaching maturity splits into 4–6 red arms. In this form it resembles an octopus. These arms gradually bend outward, so that the receptacle takes the shape of a starfish. Its lower part, 2–9 cm high and 2–5 cm wide, remains unsplit, is whitish or white-grey and porous. The outer surface of the arms is coral-red and has a reticulate-pitted structure. The inner layer is intensely cherry-red and bears a slimy layer of gleba with spores. This layer gives off an unpleasant smell of carrion similar to the smell of Phallus impudicus. During ageing the gleba dries up and turns black. On a cross-section through an arm 2–3 tubes and two wide hollows called globifers are visible. Spores: Narrowly elliptical, hyaline, measuring 4–7.5 × 2.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is believed that the original range of Clathrus archeri is Australia with Tasmania, and New Zealand. It may also be a native species on the islands of the Malay Archipelago, on Mauritius and in south-eastern Africa. From this original area it has spread to Asia and both Americas (including the state of California in the USA). In Europe it was first observed in 1914 in France. It was probably introduced with soil and plants brought from Australia to European botanical gardens and became acclimatised.
Clavaria argillacea Pers. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Clavariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Clavarioid fungi with basidiocarps forming small clusters. A single one takes the form of a club-shaped rod up to 15 cm high and 2–12 mm thick, usually straight, sometimes bent like a worm. The surface is smooth or irregularly striate, usually matt, lemon-yellow, sometimes with a grey or olive tinge. The flesh is whitish, brittle and without distinct smell and taste. Microscopic features: Hyphae colourless and transparent (hyaline), 2–15 μm wide, without clamp connections. Basidia club-shaped, up to 45–50 μm long, with a basal clamp. Spores cylindrical, thin-walled, hyaline, measuring (8–) 10–12 × 4–5 μm. Similar species: Clavaria argillacea is most easily distinguished from other clavarioid fungi by its yellowish colour and its occurrence in the company of ericaceous plants. Microscopically it is distinguished by its relatively large and cylindrical spores.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species is known only in the eastern part of North America, Europe and New Zealand. In Europe it is widely distributed; it occurs from Spain to Iceland and the northern regions of the Scandinavian Peninsula (about 68° latitude). In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – a potentially threatened species because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany and the Netherlands.
Clavulina cinerea (Bull.) J.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Height 3–6(10) cm, bushily branched. The branches are more or less grey to violet-grey, somewhat wrinkled. The tips are lighter, bluntly ended or toothed, but not flattened or crested. The base is whitish-yellowish, set off. Spore print: Light yellow. Spores spherical or elliptical, measuring 6–11 × 6–10 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is recorded in North and Central America, Europe, Japan and Australia. In Poland it is very common. It grows from August to October, in deciduous forests, less often in coniferous ones, mostly on bare ground. In Poland common.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Clavulina cinerea can easily be confused with grey-coloured varieties of Clavulina cristata or with grey forms of the more club-like Clavulina rugosa.
Clavulina coralloides (L.) J. Schröt. is a species of fungus in the family Hydnaceae. It is the type species of the genus Clavulina.

sections.head: Description
sections.text: Morphology: Young fruiting bodies are pure white, later cream, finally greyish, sometimes flesh-coloured. They reach up to 8 cm in height and 2–4 cm in width. As in other species of the family, the fruiting body is branched like a little tree. The tips of the branches are finely toothed and often darken in dry weather. The flesh is whitish, brittle, without a distinct smell, mild in taste (sometimes somewhat bitterish). Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores almost spherical, smooth, measuring 7–11 × 6.5–10 μm. Basidia 5–7 μm long with two curved sterigmata. Chemical composition: Apart from the typical fatty acids – palmitic, oleic and linoleic – Clavulina coralloides contains two unusual compounds: cis-9, cis-14-octadecadien-12-ynoic acid, and conjugated cis-9, trans-11, trans-13, cis-15-octadecatetraenoic acid. Clavulina coralloides is the only known species of fungus containing the latter compound.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Found in North America and Europe. In Poland it is common. The fruiting bodies grow singly or in clusters on the ground, sometimes on decaying wood, in coniferous and deciduous forests. It produces fruiting bodies from July to October. A saprotroph.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Similar species of Clavulina are Clavulina rugosa and Clavulina cinerea. Ramaria pallida is larger and has parallel-growing branches.
Clavulina rugosa (Bull.) J. Schröt. is a species of fungus in the family Hydnaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 0.5–1 cm. Initially club-shaped, somewhat twisted, wrinkled and longitudinally furrowed. It usually grows in groups of several fruiting bodies crowded close together. Later they divide dichotomously into several branches ending in rounded and blunt tips, sometimes with teeth. The colour of the fruiting bodies ranges from whitish through dirty white, ochre to greyish; sometimes young specimens have a violet bloom. The fruiting bodies are characterised by great variability of shape and colour. Flesh: Whitish, soft, resilient, brittle. The taste and smell are faint. Spores: Ovoid-spherical or almost spherical, smooth, colourless, measuring 9–14 × 7–12 μm. Similar species: Clavulina cinerea; it is more (repeatedly) branched and has a smoky-violet colour. Thelephora palmata; it has brown, bushily branched fruiting bodies with white tips and smells unpleasant.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It is widely distributed in North and Central America and in Europe, and also occurs in Japan and New Zealand. In Poland it is moderately common. A saprotroph. It grows on the ground in various types of forests, both in the lowlands and in the mountains, usually in small groups. The fruiting bodies appear from summer to autumn.
Climacocystis borealis (Fr.) Kotl. & Pouzar is a species of fungus in the order Polyporales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Width 5–15 cm, thickness 1–3 cm. Bulbous in young specimens, then fan-shaped. Initially it is yellow, then whitish-cream. The edge of the fruiting body is usually darker (yellow) and smooth, initially inrolled, later straight. The upper surface is scaly-felty and furrowed. It attaches to the substrate by its side or by a base somewhat resembling a stem. Sometimes neighbouring fruiting bodies fuse together. Tubes: 2–6 mm long and coloured from white to ochre. The pores are angular, 1–3 mm in diameter. The tubes form only one layer. In older specimens the pores become labyrinthine. Flesh: It is whitish, elastic, thin, soft and has a fairly pleasant smell. It forms two layers. The upper layer, 1–4 mm thick, is softer, the lower is harder. After drying the flesh becomes hard and brittle. The taste is indistinct, somewhat bitter or sour. Spores: Oval, smooth, non-amyloid, measuring 3.5–4 × 5–6 μm. They have thick-walled, spindle-shaped cystidia, sometimes ending in a cap of crystals. Similar species: Postia stiptica with a white or pinkish fruiting body. It has a very bitter taste and does not have a yellow edge.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In North America, Europe and Asia it is widely distributed, and its localities have also been reported in northern Venezuela and in Australia. In Central Europe it occurs mainly in the Alps and in other mountain ranges. In northern Germany and in Denmark it is very rare. In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Sweden. In mountain forests it is fairly common.
Clitocybe nebularis (Batsch) Kumm. is a species of fungus in the family Clitocybaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–15 cm, initially convex, later low-arched, finally flat or bent over. It usually has a broad and blunt umbo, and the margins remain inrolled for a long time. It is non-hygrophanous, fleshy and entirely white-frosted. The colour ranges from white-grey through grey to ash-grey with a brown tinge. The margin of the cap is lighter. Gills: Low, thin, crowded and decurrent on the stem. First they are white, then ochre-cream, and in older specimens brown spots appear on them. Stem: Height 6–12 cm, thickness up to 3 cm, fibrous on the outside. In young specimens club-shaped and solid, later cylindrical and cottony or hollow. At the base it always remains thickened. The colour is white to pale grey. Flesh: White, firm, fleshy, does not change colour when cut. The taste and smell are very variable. Sometimes it smells like freshly ground flour, at other times unpleasant. The smell is regarded as unpleasant by most people. Spore print: White to cream. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, colourless, measuring 6–7 × 3 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and Asia, and its occurrence has also been reported in Morocco and New Zealand. In Central Europe the species is everywhere widespread and common. It is one of the most numerous late-autumn fungi in Europe. In Poland, too, it is very common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It grows from September to November in various types of deciduous and coniferous forests. It most often occurs in lush beech forests and on needle litter in spruce forests. It often occurs together with the gąsówka fioletowawa.
Clitopilus prunulus (Scop.) P. Kumm. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Entolomataceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–10 cm, hemispherical at a young age, later arched with a sunken centre, finally becoming funnel-shaped. The margins are always inrolled. The skin is white or whitish-grey, bare and matt when dry, somewhat slimy after rain. Hymenophore: Gilled; the gills are initially white, later pinkish, crowded, low and of unequal length, running fairly deeply down the stem. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 8–18 mm, cylindrical, solid. Sometimes it grows eccentrically (i.e. not in the middle of the cap). It is fibrously grooved, frosted, and narrowed at the bottom. The colour is white. Flesh: White, soft and elastic, not changing colour when cut. The taste is insignificant, the smell resembles freshly ground flour. Spore print: Pinkish. Spores broadly spindle-shaped, measuring 10–14 × 5–6 µm. Similar species: It is often confused with Lyophyllum connatum. It differs from them in its strongly decurrent gills with a pinkish tinge and its characteristic smell.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is common in the Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone. It also occurs in Central America and Australia. In Poland it is very common. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It develops in deciduous and coniferous forests, mainly among moss. It most often occurs in better-lit places of the forest; on forest paths and roads, in clearings. It produces fruiting bodies from July to November, almost always in groups.
Coltricia perennis (L.) Murrill. is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 10 cm, funnel-shaped and very thin. The colour ranges from yellowish-brown to grey-brown, the surface is velvety, distinctly zoned, the growth zone at the margin of the cap lighter, the margin wavy. Stem: Height 2–7 cm, thickness 0.5–1 cm, centrally attached, cylindrical. The surface is velvety, rusty-yellow. Tubes: The tubes run slightly down the stem. They are up to 2 mm long and hairless. Pores 2–4 mm in diameter, whitish on young fruiting bodies, on older ones coloured from yellow-brown to grey-brown. Flesh: Elastic, cork-like, very thin. The colour is whitish, the smell imperceptible. Microscopic features: There are two kinds of hyphae: straight and weakly branched. They are rusty-brown in colour and 2–8 μm thick. Basidia measuring 15–25 × 5–7 μm, thickened, with four sterigmata. Spores ellipsoid to cylindrical in shape, light brown, smooth, somewhat dextrinoid, measuring 6–9(-10) × 3.5–5(–5.5) μm. Similar species: Coltricia cinnamomea – has a smaller cap (up to 5 cm), weakly zoned, and is very rare in Poland. The so-called Onnia tomentosa – has an unzoned, felty cap, and has setae inside the tubes

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs across the whole Northern Hemisphere, the northern limit of its range reaching Iceland and the northern edge of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In the Southern Hemisphere the occurrence of this species has been reported only in Australia and New Zealand. In Poland it is common. It occurs in coniferous and mixed forests, on dry and sandy soils. The fruiting bodies appear from summer to autumn and often persist through the winter to the following year. It is associated with such tree species as Norway spruce, silver fir and common juniper. It used to be more common, now it is rarer. It avoids calcareous soils.
Conocybe apala (Fr.) Arnolds is a species of fungus in the family Bolbitiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1–2 cm, initially thimble-shaped, later bell-shaped, never becoming flat. The margins are grooved about halfway to the centre. In older fruiting bodies the margin sometimes turns outward. The surface is smooth, coloured from white to ivory, somewhat greasy in young fruiting bodies. Gills: Crowded, narrow, adnate or almost free. Initially whitish, later darker and darker; rusty-yellowish, cinnamon, brown-pink, finally brown. Stem: Height 3–11 cm, thickness up to 2 mm. It is unevenly cylindrical, gradually thicker toward the base, hollow inside. The surface is smooth, glassy-white, longitudinally slightly grooved. No ring. Flesh: Thin and brittle, without distinct smell and taste. Spore print: Rusty-brown. Spores elliptical, smooth, with a germ pore. Size: 10–15 × 6–9 μm. Similar species: Conocybe siliginea, whose fruiting bodies change colour from pale to ochre with age. Agrocybe pediades, which has a yellow-brown cap and brown gills.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America and in Europe. In Poland its distribution and frequency are not known. In the scientific literature up to 2003 only one locality was reported (in the Nowy Targ Basin). It grows on pastures, meadows, golf courses and roadsides, in parks, mostly scattered or in small groups. The fruiting body is very delicate and short-lived; within a few hours of growing, its stem collapses, soon afterwards the fruiting body shrinks, turns brown and dries up; usually a fruiting body that grew in the morning dies by the afternoon.
Coprinellus disseminatus (Pers.) J.E. Lange is a species of fungus belonging to the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: 1–1.5 cm in diameter, in young fruiting bodies cream, light ochre, grey-yellow, beige or ochre-yellowish, bell-shaped, thimble-shaped. In mature fruiting bodies grey in various shades, broadly bell-shaped. Unlike some species of Coprinus, it does not deliquesce. The surface of the cap is finely folded radially, dry and matt. Hymenophore: Gilled, with widely spaced gills (according to some sources they are closely spaced), attached straight to the stem. The colour of the gills is white at first, then in a grey-violet or ochre shade, in older fruiting bodies they are dark, almost black. Under a lens, tiny hairs can be seen on the cap (viewed against the light). Stem: 4–5 cm long, about 0.1 cm in diameter, whitish, slightly hygrophanous, cylindrical, often curved. Flesh: Whitish, very thin, with a mild taste and a slightly mushroomy smell. Spore print: Black. The spores measure about 8–9 × 6–8 µm, are ellipsoid, smooth. Similar species: Psathyrella pygmaea – does not have hairs on the cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North, Central and South America, Europe, Asia, New Zealand and Hawaii. In Poland it is very common. A saprotroph. Its fruiting bodies grow in groups, forming dense carpets. Fungi of this species live in the dead wood of rotting stumps, sometimes also those below the surface of the soil. The fruiting bodies appear from May to November, usually several times at the same locality during one season. It happens that the fruiting bodies of this fungus also grow en masse on still-living trunks of old trees, just above the ground or even a metre above.
Coprinellus micaceus (Bull.) Vilgalys, Hopple & Jacq. Johnson is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Height:. Yellow-brownish, bell-shaped, folded and grooved, when young covered with shiny granules, remnants of the veil. In wet conditions the caps deliquesce. Gills: White in young specimens, darkening with age, finally black, but their edges remain white for a long time. They are crowded and narrowly adnate. In wet weather they deliquesce. Stem: Length , width. It is cylindrical, hollow inside, white and finely dusted in young specimens, smooth and glossy in older ones. Microscopic features: Spore print brown-black. Spores measuring , subelliptical, smooth, with a central germ pore. Basidia 4-spored, surrounded by 3–6 brachybasidioles. Pleurocystidia elliptical to ovoid or half-spindle-shaped in form and measuring. Cheilocystidia similar. Caulocystidia also occur, up to long.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed in the world. It occurs in North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and New Zealand. In Poland it is common. A terrestrial fungus and one growing on trees. It grows in forests, gardens, in parks on rotting trunks and near tree roots, from May to November, often in dense clusters.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Coprinellus disseminatus – has no shiny granules on the cap, but fibrils or small scales, remnants of the veil; it grows on rotting tree trunks. Coprinellus angulatus – hard to distinguish; it has a matt surface and the edges of the gills are not white; certain identification is given only by observation of the spores under a microscope. Mycena inclinata – similar in colour and also grows in groups on stumps, but has white gills and a smaller cap.
Coprinopsis atramentaria (Bull.) Redhead, Vilgalys & Moncalvo is a fungus of the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Height 3–8 cm, cylindrical in young individuals, later bell-shaped, at the end almost expanded. It is radially grooved, with a few petal-like scales at the top. The colour is ash-grey or grey-brown, darker in the middle. In the mature fruiting body the whole cap together with the gills deliquesces into a black liquid. Gills: Broad, crowded, with serrated edges. White in the young fruiting body, later pink, and finally black and deliquescing. Stem: Height 5–15 cm, cylindrical, hollow, easily breaking away from the cap. The surface is smooth, white, no ring. The base is distinctly pointed. Flesh: White, thin and brittle in the cap, soft and fibrous in the stem. The taste is insignificant, the smell pleasant but indistinct. Spore print: Black. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 9–10 × 5–6 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been reported in North America, Europe, Asia and New Zealand. In Poland it is very common. It occurs quite often, in gardens, meadows, forests and wasteland. The fruiting bodies appear from spring to autumn, usually in groups at the base of felled trunks or on the ground.
Coprinopsis lagopus (Fr.) Redhead, Vilgalys & Moncalvo is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1.5–5.5 cm. Height 1–3 cm. Initially cylindrical and almost completely enclosed in a universal veil covered with white bristles or hairs. However, it expands very quickly, becomes arched, and finally its margins turn outward. In older specimens the fibrils and hairs disappear, the cap becomes smooth and takes on a light grey and later mouse-grey colour. It is grooved almost to the centre. In the way typical of Coprinus-like fungi, during ripening it deliquesces, its margins become wavy and ragged, and the cap becomes thinner and thinner. Gills: Broad, free, with smooth edges. Initially whitish, later grey, finally black. Stem: Height 7–15 cm, thickness 0.3–0.7 cm. It is cylindrical, hollow, brittle. The colour is white, the surface smooth or fibrous. Flesh: White, thin, without smell and without taste. Spore print: Black. Spores elliptical, smooth, dextrinoid, with a wide germ pore. They grow 4 per basidium. They measure 14–10 × 6–8.5 μm. Similar species: There are many similar species of Coprinus-like fungi. Reliable distinction between them is often impossible without microscopic examination. Very similar are e.g.:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, and Australia and New Zealand. In the scientific literature many of its localities have been reported across the whole of Poland. A common species, but it usually grows singly. Because of its small size and unshowy colour it is often unnoticed. It grows in forests, in gardens, on meadows. A saprotroph. Sometimes it grows on the ground, but in reality its mycelium develops on pieces of wood buried in it, sawdust and other materials containing lignin.
Coprinopsis picacea (Bull.) Redhead, Vilgalys & Moncalvo is a species of fungus belonging to the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: When mature it reaches a diameter of 3–7 cm and a height of 7–12 cm. Initially it is ovoid, then bell-shaped, then its margins turn outward and, in the way typical of Coprinus-like fungi, the fruiting body turns black and during ripening deliquesces into a black liquid. The surface is very dark, grey-brown, shiny, covered with silvery-white fibrils which separate into patches as the cap expands. Gills: Free or slightly adnate, crowded, initially white, then reddish, and then black and turning into a black liquid. Stem: Height 10–20 cm, diameter 0.7–1.5 cm, cylindrical with a bulbous base, hollow. The surface is white, flocculose. Microscopic features: Spore print black. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 13–19 × 9–12 µm; with a central germ pore.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It occurs in Europe, North America, Africa and south-eastern Asia. W. Wojewoda in 2003, in his study, gives 7 localities of Coprinopsis picacea in Poland. Numerous and more up-to-date localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. Coprinopsis picacea is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status V – a vulnerable species, which will probably soon move to the endangered category if the threat factors continue to operate. A saprotroph. It occurs among fallen leaves in forests, especially beech forests, less often under oaks and hornbeams.
Coprinus comatus (O.F. Müll.) Pers. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Height 5–10 cm, initially cylindrical, later bell-shaped. In the mature fruiting body the cap cracks radially, its margin opens and lifts, and the whole cap together with the gills deliquesces into a black liquid. It is white and fibrously scaly, only the tip is ochre and bare. Gills: White in the young fruiting body, later pink, and finally black, crowded and thin. Stem: Height 10–20 cm, thickness 0.8–2 cm. It is cylindrical, hollow, easily breaking away from the cap, somewhat rooting. The surface is smooth, white, with a movable ring. Flesh: White, thin and brittle in the cap, soft and fibrous in the stem. The taste is insignificant, the smell pleasant but indistinct. Spore print: Black. Spores measuring 10–15 × 6–8 µm, elliptical, smooth, black. Similar species: Coprinus comatus can be confused with Coprinopsis atramentaria, which differs in that its cap is smooth and grey in colour. Both species have almost the same places of occurrence.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Africa and Antarctica. In Poland it is a very common fungus. It occurs quite often in close proximity to humans, in home gardens, housing-estate lawns, on river banks, on rubbish heaps and other ruderal habitats, and also on meadows, pastures and in forests. It produces fruiting bodies from April to November.
Trametes trogii Berk. is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual, usually attaching to the substrate by its side, only rarely spread out. It has a semicircular, elongated shape, up to 12 cm wide, 2–4 cm thick, and on a cross-section it has a triangular profile (the base is attached to the substrate). The upper surface is unzoned or slightly zoned, covered with hairs 1–2 mm long. They are whitish in colour, but greyish or rusty-brown at the top. Young fruiting bodies are uniformly hairy, in older ones tufts form that give the fruiting body a rough appearance. The margin of the fruiting body is sharp. The hymenophore is tubular. The pores are fairly large, with 15–20 per cm. They are the colour of dark honey. The tubes are up to 1 cm long. The flesh is distinctly radially fibrous, pale grey-ochre in colour. After drying it fades, and under the action of KOH it changes colour to dark brown. Microscopic features: Generative hyphae thin-walled with clamp connections, rarely branched, non-amyloid. They have a diameter of (2) 2.3–2.5 (4) μm. Hyphae in the flesh are arranged radially, hyphae in the outer layers of the fruiting body are thick-walled (walls up to 2 μm thick) and slightly amyloid. Basidia thick-walled, with 4 sterigmata. They measure 18–23 × 6–7.5 μm. No cystidia.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs only in the Northern Hemisphere: in North America, Europe and Asia. In Europe it is widely distributed, but it does not occur in all countries – it has not been recorded in England and Denmark. It occurs more often in warmer regions; on the Scandinavian Peninsula it is very rare. In Poland, too, it is not common. A saprotroph growing on dead wood. It most often occurs on poplars and willows, but its occurrence has also been recorded on many other deciduous tree species (maple, birch, beech, oak and elm).
Cortinarius armillatus (Fr.) Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Cortinariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter of the cap 5–15 cm. It is non-hygrophanous. The shape in young fruiting bodies is hemispherical, later arched, finally expanded with a blunt and broad umbo. The margin remains inrolled for a long time. The surface of young fruiting bodies is radially fibrillose, of older ones scaly-fibrous. At the margins there are remnants of a red cortina. The colour is rusty-brown, cinnamon-reddish or reddish. A characteristic feature of this species is the frequently encountered bell shape of the cap. Gills: Broad, slightly notched with a tooth, with whitish and slightly scalloped edges. In young specimens they are light ochre, in older ones red-brown. Stem: Height 7–16 cm, thickness 1–4 cm, cylindrical, the base bulbously thickened. It is solid. The surface is light violet-brown, covered with brick-coloured, fibrous veil remnants, which as the stem grows usually form numerous bands. The base is white and felty. Flesh: Coloured from whitish-yellow-reddish to pale brown. The taste is mild, the smell indistinct. Microscopic features: Spore print rusty-brown. Spores measuring 9–12 × 5–7 μm, ellipsoid, finely warted, moderately amyloid. Their wall thickness is about 0.75 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Its occurrence has been described in North America, Europe, Korea, Japan and in central Africa. In regions where it finds favourable conditions, e.g. in the forests of Scandinavia or Bavaria, it often occurs in great numbers. In Poland it is a fairly common species. It grows on the ground, in deciduous and mixed forests, thickets, by roads. It forms fruiting bodies from July to October.
Cortinarius bolaris (Pers.) Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Cortinariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–6 cm, shape initially hemispherical or arched, later convex, older specimens become flat. The surface is light yellowish, covered with scales coloured from cinnabar-red to saffron-red. In dry weather the cap fades. The surface is dry, non-hygrophanous. Gills: Initially cream-yellow or pale ochre-yellow, with time they darken and become fawn-rusty, finally light cinnamon. They are slightly adnate to the stem and fairly crowded. Stem: Height 4–8 cm, thickness up to 1.5 cm, cylindrical. Solid in young specimens, hollow in older ones. The surface under the cap is white-cream and slightly scaly; otherwise it is whitish-yellowish and covered fairly densely with cinnabar-red fibrils and scales. The base is darker, dark red. Flesh: Whitish in the cap, yellowish or ochre in the stem, even darker at the base, grey-yellow. With time it gradually darkens more and more and becomes red-brown. The taste and smell are indistinct. Microscopic features: Spore print red-brown. Spores ovoid or almost spherical, slightly warty, measuring 6–8 × 5–6 μm. No pleurocystidia. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed in the eastern part of North America and has also been recorded in Costa Rica. It also occurs in most countries of Europe. A mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in deciduous and mixed forests, on the ground, among moss. In Poland it produces fruiting bodies from August to November. It grows almost exclusively under beeches, rarely under oaks. It prefers acidic soils. It usually occurs singly, only sometimes forming small groups of fruiting bodies and.
Cortinarius caperatus (Pers.) Fr. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Cortinariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–12 cm, in young fungi ovoid and hemispherical, later broadly bell-shaped, in older ones flat with a blunt umbo. Young fruiting bodies are frosted. In dry weather it becomes wrinkled and cracked at the margins. Initially it is grey-violet, greyish, with veil remnants at the margins. Older specimens range in colour from leather-yellow to beige-brown. Gills: Clay-yellow in the young fruiting body, later rusty-brownish, crowded, notched with a tooth, initially covered by a white veil. Stem: Height 7–15 cm, thickness 1–3 cm. It is cylindrical, solid, bulbously widened at the base. It has a narrow whitish-yellowish ring, above which it is flaky, below fibrous and striate. The colour ranges from whitish through cream to ochre. Flesh: White or pale cream. The taste is insignificant, the smell indistinct. Spore print: Rusty-yellow. Spores almond-shaped and warted, 11–14 × 7–9 µm. Similar species: Young fruiting bodies with a silvery-violet cap are similar to Cortinarius traganus, but this one has an unpleasant smell and gills covered by a cortina.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described only in North America and Europe. In Central Europe, especially in the northern regions, it is fairly common, in others rare. In Poland, too, it is common only in some areas. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in spruce and pine forests on poor and acidic sandy soils, both damp and dry. It often occurs in the vicinity of the lichen chrobotek kubkowaty and the moss bielistka siwa. It does not occur at all on calcareous substrate. In Poland the fruiting bodies appear from July to October.
Cortinarius mucosus (Bull.) E. Berger is a species of fungus in the family Cortinariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter of the cap from 4 to 12 cm, hemispherical when young, then arched, finally expanded. The colour ranges from yellow-brown to light chestnut-brown. In wet weather sticky, slimy and glutinous, in dry weather shiny. Gills: From whitish to clay-brownish, usually narrow and decurrent on the stem, or adnate to it. Stem: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 8–18 mm, cylindrical, solid, sometimes only thickened at the base. Usually up to 2/3 of its height it is covered with a white and slippery veil, above which it is browning. Flesh: Whitish to cream, without taste and smell. Spore print: Rusty-brown. Spores ellipsoid or almond-shaped, smooth, measuring 12–15 × 6–7 μm. Similar species: Cortinarius collinitus. It differs little in appearance: it has only a slightly different cap colour (from yellow-orange to brown-orange) and a violet-brown stem, often narrowed at the bottom. It grows only under spruces; Cortinarius trivialis. It has an ochre-yellow-brown cap and rolls of slime on the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed in the northern part of North America and in Europe. In Europe its northern limit of range reaches as far as the Svalbard archipelago in the Arctic. In Poland it is common. A terrestrial mycorrhizal fungus. It grows mainly in pine forests on sandy soils. In places it occurs commonly. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November.
Cortinarius semisanguineus (Fr.) Gillet is a species of fungus belonging to the family Cortinariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1–6 cm, convex when young, convex-flattened when older, often with an umbo, smooth or scaly. Matt when young, later bare and shiny. The colour ranges from cinnamon through olive-brown to cinnamon-brown. Gills: They are up to 10 mm wide. They are sinuately adnate, closely spaced, initially blood-red, later brown-reddish, with lighter edges. Stem: 3–7 cm long, 4–6 mm thick, cylindrical, fibrous at the base. It is yellowish or yellow-ochre in colour, often reddened at the base. Flesh: Yellowish in colour, reddish and fibrous at the base. Spore print: Rusty-brown. Spores elliptical, with fine warts; measuring 6.5–8 × 4.5–5 µm. Similar species: Cortinarius cinnamomeus. It is distinguished by cinnamon-yellow scales on the cap. Cortinarius purpureus. It has a red-brown cap and the stem is almost entirely red and fibrous. Laccaria laccata, which has widely spaced gills and a white spore print.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe and New Zealand. In Poland it is common. It grows from August to October, mainly in coniferous forests, under spruces and pines; it can only rarely be met under deciduous trees (beech, oak, birch). It occurs both in the lowlands and in the mountains. It is fairly common.
Cortinarius violaceus (L.) Gray is a species of fungus in the family Cortinariaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter on average from 4 to 15 cm< Young specimens have fruiting bodies of an intense blue-violet colour with a slightly metallic sheen. In older specimens the colour is brown with a violet tinge. The surface is granular, dry, velvety. The shape is semicircular, flat in older ones. Gills: The spacing is quite variable in this species, from sparse to moderately crowded; broad and broadly adnate, coloured from violet in young individuals, through violet-brown to dark brown in older ones. The edges of the gills are covered with fibrils (this can be seen only under a lens). Stem: Height 8–12 cm, thickness 1–3 cm. The shape is club-like with a distinctly thickened base (reaching a thickness of about 4 cm). Solid in young specimens, hollow inside in older ones. The surface is scaly, dark violet, and in dry weather almost black. In young specimens it is surrounded by a cortina, which however quickly disappears. Flesh: The colour is from light to dark violet, with a mild taste and a cedar smell. A base stains the flesh red, an acid greenish. Spore print: Brown. Microscopic features: Spores almond-shaped or ellipsoid, finely warty, measuring 11.5–13.5 × 7–9 µm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on some islands and on all continents except Africa and Antarctica. In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status V – vulnerable. It is also on lists of threatened species in Belgium, Germany, Denmark, England and the Netherlands. It grows on the ground in deciduous and mixed forests, singly or in small groups in the summer–autumn period (from August to October). It grows mainly under beeches and birches, on acidic or alkaline soils. It is found mainly in the mountains.
Craterellus cornucopioides (L.) Pers. is a species of fungus in the family Hydnaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Diameter 3–8 cm, trumpet-funnel-shaped with an inrolled margin, wavy in mature specimens. The inner part is initially brown-black, later black-grey, finally black, with irregular sparse scales. The outer part is grey-brown, first smooth, then wrinkled. The outer side of the whole fruiting body is covered by the hymenium, and therefore in mature specimens the white spores colour it white. It is hygrophanous. Stem: Height 5–12 cm. It is hollow inside, widening in a funnel shape from the bottom upward, passing smoothly into the cap. In the upper part it is often torn. The surface is smooth or wrinkled, grey-brown or grey-black in colour. Older stems, like the cap, are dusted white with spores. Flesh: Thin, at first grey-black, then entirely black. It is fairly elastic and springy. After drying it becomes brittle, but after soaking it regains its elasticity. The taste is insignificant, the smell pleasant. Spore print: White. Spores 12–15 × 7–8.5 µm, smooth, colourless.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: It is hard to confuse with another fungus because of its characteristic appearance and the lack of similar species. The most similar is Craterellus undulatus.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs almost exclusively in the Northern Hemisphere: in North and Central America, Europe and Asia. Its northern range reaches the central part of the Scandinavian Peninsula and Hudson Bay in Canada. In the Southern Hemisphere it occurs only on the island of New Guinea. A mycorrhizal fungus. In Poland it produces fruiting bodies from August to November in deciduous and mixed forests, usually in clumps, most often in foothill areas. It usually grows under beeches and oaks.
Craterellus tubaeformis (Fr.) Quél. is a species of fungus in the family Hydnaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–6 cm, trumpet-shaped and deeply umbilicate, with thin flesh and a strongly wavy margin, which in old age often opens into the hollow stem. The colour of the cap ranges from yellow-brown to grey-brown. Hymenophore: In the form of ridges clearly running down the stem. Young ridges are often beautifully yellow, later yellow-grey or white-grey; narrow, thick, sparse, dichotomously branched with numerous transverse connections (anastomoses), running down the stem. Stem: Height 4–8 cm, thickness 0.4–1 cm. It is irregularly cylindrical and longitudinally flattened and wrinkled and distinctly hollow. Ochre-yellow at the bottom, greyish at the top. Flesh: Yellowish-grey, with a mild taste. The smell is hardly perceptible, often somewhat earthy-musty. Spore print: Cream-yellow, non-amyloid. Spores spherical, smooth and almost colourless, 9–12 × 5–10 µm. Similar species: Craterellus tubaeformis can be confused with Craterellus lutescens, which has a golden-yellow stem and grey-whitish and weakly developed ridges. Cantharellus cinereus is also similar, but it has a black-brown stem and cap and ridges with a bluish bloom.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Asia, Australia and on some islands, and its locality has also been reported in Antarctica. In Poland it is fairly common. A terrestrial fungus, growing usually in groups in coniferous and deciduous forests in damp places overgrown with moss. It grows both on acidic soils and on soils containing calcium. Most often, however, it occurs in mountain forests under spruces and firs. It occurs in the company of spruces (both living trees and dead remains). It occurs on acidic soils. It appears in late autumn and occurs until the first frosts.
Crepidotus mollis (Schaeff.) Staude is a species of fungus belonging to the family Crepidotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual, 0.5–3 cm in diameter and 3–5 mm thick. The stem is small and occurs only in young fruiting bodies, later disappearing. The fruiting body is kidney-shaped or shell-shaped, thin and attached by its side, the margins inrolled in young specimens. The surface is coloured from white to grey-ochre, smooth, matt. The skin can be easily peeled off. Under the skin there is a gelatinous layer, giving the fruiting body resilience and softness. The hymenophore is gilled. The gills radiate from the point where the cap attaches to the substrate. They are crowded and thin, cream in young specimens, cinnamon-brown in older ones, finally grey-brown. The edges of the gills are covered with a gelatinous layer (the same as in the cap under the skin). Flesh: thin, white, with a mild taste and indistinct smell. Spore print: Brown. Spores broadly elliptical, smooth, measuring 7–9 × 5–7 μm. Microscopic features: Basidia 12–30 × 6–9 µm, cylindrical-club-shaped, 4-spored. Spores 7.0–10.0 × 5.0–6.0 (–6.5) µm, Q = 1.42–1.82, ellipsoid, almond-shaped in side view, smooth, yellowish-brown in KOH, thick-walled, usually with one, less often two large and several small guttules, thin-walled.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents and on many islands. In Poland it is common. A fungus growing on trees, occurring in deciduous and mixed forests, also in parks, on meadows, in the mountains mainly in the lower parts. It grows on dead wood of deciduous trees (on twigs, trunks). It occurs in groups, the fruiting bodies appear from May to October. It occurs on: horse chestnut, aspen and oak.
Crucibulum laeve (Huds.) Kambly is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Young fruiting bodies are roundish or somewhat cylindrical, with a felty, roughly tomentose surface and a colour from yellowish through dirty orange to cinnamon. When mature they take the shape of a thick-walled cup, bowl or crucible and are covered with a whitish epiphragm, which on splitting reveals numerous lens-shaped peridioles enclosed in a thick, cream-white tunic. Initially they are light ochre, later whitish. They are connected to the peridium by a little cord attached in the middle part of the lower side of the peridiole (at this spot there is a small bump on it). With time the cords disappear, and then the peridioles are immersed in a drop of slimy substance filling the bottom of the peridium. The peridium is thick, single-layered, smooth on the inside, shiny, even, greyish-white in colour, and felty on the outside. The opening of the peridium is round and even, and the epiphragm closing it is two-layered; the outer layer is felty and of the same colour as the peridium, the inner layer is white. Sometimes after the epiphragm splits, remnants of it remain at the edge of the opening. This species is characterised by great morphological variability.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widely distributed mainly in the Northern Hemisphere (North and Central America, Europe, Asia), but it also occurs in Australia and New Zealand. In Poland the species is common. It grows on wood remains, on fallen twigs. It can be found in forests and thickets, by streams, by roads, in parks. The fruiting bodies appear from summer to autumn. A saprotroph, a coprophilous fungus.
Cuphophyllus virgineus (Wulfen) Kovalenko is a species of fungus in the family Cuphophyllaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter from 2 to 4.5 cm, young – hemispherical, convex, later flat, and somewhat sunken in the middle. In damp conditions pale yellow to watery white, somewhat sticky, in drought snow-white. Gills: Sparse, decurrent on the stem, broad at the base, thin at the edge, watery, whitish-yellowish. Stem: Height from 1.5 to 4.5 cm, diameter from 3 to 5 mm, equal in thickness, narrowed and flattened toward the base, initially solid, later hollow, white in colour, sometimes with a pink bloom. Flesh: Watery white, no smell, mild taste. Spore print: White. Similar species: Because of its characteristic appearance and place of growth, confusion is unlikely.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Polish scientific literature it has been described at numerous localities. A terrestrial saprotrophic fungus. It appears from September to November. Fairly common, it grows on damp pastures and meadows and grass-covered forest roads.
Cyanoboletus pulverulentus (Opat.) Gelardi, Vizzini & Simonini is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–12(15) cm, red-brown or chestnut-brown. The skin is matt, delicately velvety, fairly dry. Tubes: Lemon-yellow, fairly short, glossy, very sensitive to pressure, immediately turning dark blue. Stem: Hazel-coloured, yellowish in the upper part, almost always slender. The surface is delicately granular-fibrillose, never reticulate. When cut or pressed it turns intensely blue. Flesh: Yellow, immediately turning dark blue to blue-black when cut. Fleshy and firm. In older individuals dry and rough. Spores: Smooth, 10–16 × 4–6 µm, without a germ pore. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It occurs in North, Central and South America, Europe, Australia and Asia (in the latter it is known only in Korea and Japan). In Poland the species is rare. It is on the Red List of Plants and Fungi of Poland. It has the status R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographic range and small habitat areas. In Poland it produces fruiting bodies from July to October,. It grows under oaks, beeches, less often pines.
Cyanosporus caesius (Schrad.) McGinty is a species of fungus in the order Polyporales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual. It attaches to the substrate by its side. Diameter 1–5 cm, exceptionally up to 8 cm, width 0.3–1 cm, bracket-shaped and sometimes thickened at the base, less often spread out and reflexed. The margin is thin, wavy and slightly inrolled. The surface is felty, rough or hairy, weakly striate. On older fruiting bodies a characteristic fine net appears. Young fruiting bodies are white, turning blue-grey to dark grey when touched; older fruiting bodies remain blue-grey to dark grey throughout. The margin of the fruiting body (growth zone) remains white throughout. Hymenophore: Tubular, coloured from white to grey-blue. It turns blue when touched. The tubes are 0.5–4.5 mm long and sometimes run down the substrate. The pores are 0.15–0.3 mm in diameter, exceptionally 0.4 mm, with 3–4 per 1 mm. They range in shape from round to angular and have bluish edges, ragged in older fruiting bodies. Flesh: Whitish, turning blue when damaged, weakly zoned and fairly firm. The taste and smell are indistinct. Spore print: Blue-grey. Spores cylindrical, slightly curved, colourless, with a smooth surface and with 2 droplets. Size 3.5–5.5 × 1–1.5 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and South America, Europe, Asia and New Zealand. In Poland it is very common. It grows in coniferous and mixed forests, above all in the mountains, much less often in the lowlands. It can be found mainly on Norway spruce, silver fir and Scots pine. It has also been recorded on fir species grown as ornamental plants: grand fir and Abies nordmanniana, less often on deciduous trees (on beech and hornbeam). Sometimes it also occurs on wooden structures. It is fairly common.
Cyathus olla (Batsch) Pers. is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Goblet-shaped or cup-shaped, 0.8–1.2 cm high and 0.5–1 cm wide. Young individuals are completely closed and have a convex and rounded top. When ripe the top of the cup opens, revealing the interior with peridioles. The outer surface is delicately hairy, initially ochre or light brown in colour, later greyish. The inner surface of the cup is smooth, bare, shiny and ash-grey. The peridioles are disc-shaped, usually shiny. They are whitish or greyish in colour and 2–3.5 mm in size. They are attached to the fruiting body by thin cords (funiculus). Spores: Colourless, ellipsoid or ovoid, measuring 8–13 × 5–8 μm. Similar species: In Poland there are two more cups similar in size and shape: Cyathus striatus, which is strongly spiny on the outside and striate on the inside, and Cyathus stercoreus, which also has a spiny outer surface and grows on animal droppings.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A cosmopolitan species; apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland the species is common. It grows on the ground, on wood remains of various tree species, both deciduous and coniferous, and also on leaves, remains of straw and other plant remains. It can be found in forests, in fields and in gardens, and even in flats and on balconies (e.g. on rotting wood). The fruiting bodies appear from summer to autumn, usually in groups.
Cyathus striatus (Huds.) Willd is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Cup-shaped, 1–2 cm high and 0.8–1 cm wide. The outer side is rusty-brown, brown or almost black and is strongly hairy. The margin is sometimes slightly turned out. The inner side is without hairs, smooth and distinctly longitudinally striate, which is a characteristic feature of the species. It is silvery-shiny. In mature specimens inside the cup there are disc-shaped, grey or grey-brown peridioles 1.5–2 mm in diameter. They are attached to the fruiting body by thin cords (funiculus). Spores: Numbering 10–15, ovoid or lens-shaped, colourless. Size: 18–22 × 8–12 μm. Similar species: In Poland there occurs the somewhat similar Cyathus olla, which on the outside is silky-fibrous, and inside without striations.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is distributed worldwide. Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, also on many islands. In Europe its northern limit of range runs through the 64th parallel of latitude. In Poland it is a common species. It grows on wood remains of various tree species, both deciduous and coniferous, and also on leaves and other plant remains. It most often occurs in damp thickets and forests. The fruiting bodies grow in summer and autumn, singly or in groups. A saprotroph.
Cystoderma amianthinum (Scop.) Fayod is a species of fungus belonging to the family Squamanitaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: It produces many forms and is variable in colouring. Forms with entirely white caps are encountered. Cap: Diameter 2–5 cm. Semicircular in young fruiting bodies, then arched, finally flat. Fibrils, remnants of the veil, hang from the margins. It is radially wrinkled, non-hygrophanous. The surface is dry, granular, initially pale yellow, later ochre and golden-ochre. Gills: Up to 4 mm wide, crowded, slightly notched at the stem. White in young specimens, later ochre-yellowish. Stem: Height 4–6 cm, thickness 2–5 mm. It is fragile, cylindrical, thickened in the lower part, sometimes curved, initially solid, later hollow inside. The surface is the same colour as the cap. In the upper part there is a small, rising ring, whitish and lumpy-fibrillose. Above the ring it is bare, below it is covered with spreading scales. Flesh: Yellowish. Soft in the cap, firm in the stem. The smell is unpleasant, earthy. Spore print: White, amyloid. Spores 4–6 × 3–4 µm in diameter. Similar species: It is distinguished from other Cystoderma by its ochre colouring, and from lepiotas by its ring and granular cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Cystoderma amianthinum is widely distributed in North America and Europe. From Asia its occurrence has been described only in Japan and in Magadan Oblast in the far east of Russia. It also occurs in Australia and on some islands. In Poland the species is common, occurring across the whole country. A terrestrial fungus. It grows in light coniferous and mixed forests, in clearings, among moss, under pines, spruces, beeches, in thickets, on heaths, and is also found on pastures. The fruiting bodies appear from August to November.
Daedaleopsis confragosa (Bolton) J. Schröt. is a species of fungus belonging to the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Diameter 5–15 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, shell-shaped, semicircular. No stem; it attaches to the substrate by its side. The colouring is variable: light grey, ochre-brown, wine-red or black-red. Concentric zoning of the same colour often occurs. The skin is bare, the upper surface of the fruiting body usually uneven and wrinkled. The margin of the fruiting body is very sharp and thin. Hymenophore: In the form of elongated, angular, labyrinthine-gill-like tubes arranged radially. Sometimes at the base they pass into gills. They are 0.5–1.5 cm long and whitish or greyish. Their characteristic feature is that when pressed they change colour to flesh-pink. Flesh: Pale brownish, elastic, of cork-like consistency. Young specimens have a sour smell, older ones are odourless. Spore print: White. Spores cylindrical, slightly curved, with a narrowed and pointed base with 2–3 fat droplets. Size: (6)8–11 × (1.5)2–3 µm. Similar species: Trametes versicolor has a similarly zoned but more colourful cap; it also differs completely in its hymenophore.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Daedaleopsis confragosa is widely distributed across the whole Northern Hemisphere. In Central Europe it is common, in Poland as well. A fungus growing on deciduous trees. It grows most often on various species of willow, on alder and birch. It attacks mainly dead trees, but sometimes also weakened, living trees. The fruiting body is annual.
Podofomes mollis (Sommerf.) Gorjón is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: A polyporoid fungus forming spread-out or sessile fruiting bodies up to 0.6 cm thick and up to 17 cm long. Sometimes they have margins reflexed for about 2 cm. The upper surface of the fruiting body is bristly or velvety and coloured from brown to black. On it there are darker, grooved streaks on stiff hairs. The hymenophore is tubular, dirty beige, yellowish-brown, greyish. The tubes are 0.5–5 mm long, their pores 1–2 mm in diameter and irregular in shape, slightly elongated or polygonal. The flesh is pale brown. The spore print is coloured from light to dark brown. Spores cylindrical, measuring 8–10 × 2.5–3.5 μm. Microscopic features: Hyphal system trimitic. Generative hyphae of the context hyaline, thin-walled, with clamp connections, 2.5–4 µm in diameter. Skeletal hyphae of the context thick-walled, without septa, those in the lower layer of the context pale greenish-brown in KOH, those in the upper, dark layer darker and brown in KOH, 2.5–4 µm in diameter. Binding hyphae of the context thick-walled, without septa, strongly branched, 2–3 µm in diameter. Hyphae of the trama similar to those in the lower layer of the context.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In the scientific literature for Poland very numerous localities have been reported. Numerous and more up-to-date localities are also given by the online mushroom atlas. It is classed there among threatened species worthy of protection. A saprotrophic fungus growing on trees. Habitat: deciduous and mixed forests, parks. It develops on dead deciduous wood of such species as maples, beeches, poplars and oaks. It produces fruiting bodies from January to October (depending on the weather). It causes white rot of wood.
Delicatula integrella (Pers.) Fayod is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–12 mm, initially hemispherical, then expanded, finally strongly concave, translucent with a sharp, toothed margin. The surface is whitish, bare and smooth. Hymenophore: Gill-vein-like. The gill-veins are narrow, sparse, sometimes branching and anastomosing, adnate and slightly decurrent on the stem. Stem: Thread-like, 10–15 mm high and 0.5–1 mm thick. The base is bulbous with delicate mycelium. The surface is white. Flesh: Soft, membranous, without distinct smell, with a mild taste. Microscopic features: Spores ellipsoid, ovoid, lemon-shaped or almond-shaped, smooth, 7.5–8.5 × 4–5 µm, amyloid. Similar species: A characteristic feature of Delicatula integrella is its poorly developed, vein-like gills (so-called gill-veins). Some species of the genus Hemimycena (white bonnets) are similar, small and white, but they have well-developed gills. Mycena epipterygia has lemon-coloured shades.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Delicatula integrella occurs on all continents except Antarctica. In Europe it occurs throughout the area, apart from the Balkans. In Poland, W. Wojewoda in 2003 cited many localities, noting that the frequency of occurrence and degree of threat are not known. More up-to-date and numerous localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. It is included there in the list of threatened species worthy of protection.
Dissingia leucomelaena (Pers.) K. Hansen & X.H. Wang is a species of fungus in the family Helvellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Of the apothecium type, 1.5–4 cm wide, sessile or with a short stem, urn-shaped or cup-shaped. In older specimens the margin often splits in a star shape. The hymenial (inner) surface is matt, grey-brown to black-brown, bare; the outer surface is whitish at the base, matt grey to black-brown, delicately hairy above (visible only through a lens). The stem, if present, is very short, consisting of whitish folds or blunt ribs. The flesh is thin, brittle, about 1.0 mm thick, two-layered, watery grey and whitish, with a mild smell and taste. Microscopic features: Spores 21.0–25.0 × 11.5–13.0 µm, elliptical, smooth, thin-walled, non-amyloid, with a single oil droplet when mature. Similar species: Dissingia leucomelaena has fruiting bodies similar to those of cup fungi of the genus Peziza. It is distinguished from them by the colour of the cup; the inner surface is matt, grey-black to dark grey-brown, the outer grey-black-white. Helvella queletii is similar, but it has a distinct, ribbed, white stem whose ribs extend to the base of the cup, and it also differs in colour; the outer is lighter than the inner.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Dissingia leucomelaena occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. In Europe it is widely distributed and many of its localities have been reported from the Mediterranean to the northern regions of the Scandinavian Peninsula. M.A. Chmiel in 2006 cited 3 localities in Poland, but in later years others have been reported. Numerous and current localities are also given by the online mushroom atlas. It is included there in the list of threatened species worthy of protection. A terrestrial fungus. It occurs singly or scattered on soil among conifer needles, especially in mountain and coastal forests.
Echinoderma asperum (Pers.) Bon is a species of fungus in the family Agaricaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter from 5 to 12 cm. When young it is bell-shaped to convex, later flatly expanded. In old fruiting bodies concave in the middle, fleshy, concentrically covered with blackish-brown spreading scales that fall off. The colour is brown, darker in the middle. In the middle of the cap there are blackish-brown pointed and spreading scales, which fall off in older fruiting bodies. Gills: Crowded, white to cream, forked at the ends. Stem: Height from 4 to 8 cm, diameter from 0.7 to 1.5 cm. It is cylindrical, bulbously widened at the base, firm and compact. Initially solid, later hollow, in the lower part brown, fibrous to scaly. A broad membranous ring, in mature specimens hanging, ragged, whitish on top, brownish underneath. Flesh: Soft in the cap, rather fibrous in the stem, whitish. It has a penetrating unpleasant "spicy" smell (like Scleroderma citrinum) and a sour taste. Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores long-elliptical, smooth, measuring 6.5–11 × 2–3.5 μm, weakly amyloid. Cheilocystidia ellipsoid or almost round, measuring up to about 30 × 15 μm. No pleurocystidia. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In the Northern Hemisphere it is widely distributed, occurring in North America, Europe and Asia, and in the south only in the southern part of North America and in Australia. A terrestrial saprotroph. It grows in coniferous and deciduous forests, in parks, thickets and gardens. It likes shady and damper places. It produces fruiting bodies from August to October.
Erythricium aurantiacum (Lasch) D. Hawksw. & A. Henrici is a species of fungus in the family Corticiaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: The anamorph forms bulbous sclerotia 70–100 µm in diameter, occurring singly or in small clusters, light orange, without a cortex, developing on the surface of the host's thallus, which as a result is considerably degraded. The teleomorph forms a light orange, spread-out, thin basidiocarp up to about 10 mm in diameter, with a granular to flocculose surface, closely adhering to the surface of the host's thallus, with an indefinite margin. The hymenium consists of one or several layers of basidia on vertically branched, thin-walled hyphae. Basidia 25–40 × 12–15 mm, distinctly wider than the hyphae supporting them, initially narrowly cylindrical, sometimes with a basal or lateral, ellipsoid probasidial vesicle, on reaching maturity usually becoming club-shaped, sometimes with one thin, transverse septum in the upper 1/3. No basal clamp connections, the basal septum with a dolipore visible under the light microscope. Each basidium has 4 sterigmata up to 6.5 µm long and 3 µm wide at the base, curved.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
